title: Bisoprolol fumarate tablets, USP: full prescribing information
authors: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, Inc.; Harman Finochem Ltd
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved prescribing information, published in DailyMed; structured product labelling version 4, published 19 October 2026
funder: not stated; FDA-approved labelling carries no funding statement. The labeller submits the text and the Food and Drug Administration approves it.
result: Indicated in the management of hypertension, alone or with other antihypertensive agents; the usual starting dose is 5 mg once daily, 2.5 mg in some patients, increased to 10 mg and if necessary 20 mg. A beta1-selective (cardioselective) adrenoceptor blocking agent without significant membrane-stabilising or intrinsic sympathomimetic activity in its therapeutic dosage range; cardioselectivity is not absolute and at doses of 20 mg or more bisoprolol also inhibits beta2 adrenoceptors, chiefly in bronchial and vascular musculature, so the lowest effective dose is important. It is a racemic mixture and the S(-) enantiomer carries most of the beta-blocking activity. Absolute bioavailability after 10 mg is about 80%, first-pass metabolism about 20%, serum protein binding about 30%, peak concentrations at 2 to 4 hours, plasma elimination half-life 9 to 12 hours and steady state within 5 days of once-daily dosing. Bisoprolol is eliminated equally by renal and non-renal pathways, with about 50% of the dose appearing unchanged in the urine and the remainder as inactive metabolites, and it is not metabolised by cytochrome P450 II D6 (debrisoquin hydroxylase). With creatinine clearance below 40 ml/min the plasma half-life is increased about threefold, and in cirrhosis the half-life ranges from 8.3 to 21.7 hours. The most prominent effect is negative chronotropy, reducing resting and exercise heart rate, with a fall in cardiac output and little change in stroke volume; electrophysiology studies in man show that bisoprolol significantly decreases heart rate, increases sinus node recovery time, prolongs atrioventricular node refractory periods and prolongs atrioventricular nodal conduction during rapid atrial stimulation. The mechanism of the antihypertensive effect has not been completely established; decreased cardiac output, inhibition of renin release by the kidneys and diminished tonic sympathetic outflow may be involved. In placebo-controlled US trials of mild-to-moderate hypertension, placebo-subtracted falls in sitting pressure after 3 to 4 weeks were 5.0/4.8 mm Hg at 5 mg, 5.8/7.7 at 10 mg and 7.4/8.7 at 20 mg, with placebo-subtracted heart-rate reductions of 6.7, 8.2 and 10.8 beats per minute; blood pressure returned to baseline when bisoprolol was tapered over two weeks in a long-term study. Pulmonary function studies in healthy volunteers, asthmatics and patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease found slight asymptomatic increases in airways resistance and decreases in forced expiratory volume at 20 mg and higher, similar to other cardioselective beta-blockers and reversed by bronchodilator therapy. Warnings: exacerbation of angina pectoris and, in some instances, myocardial infarction or ventricular arrhythmia have been observed in patients with coronary artery disease after abrupt cessation of beta-blocker therapy, so patients are cautioned against interruption without medical advice, therapy is tapered over approximately one week under careful observation even without overt coronary artery disease, and treatment is reinstituted at least temporarily if withdrawal symptoms occur; beta-blockers may mask some manifestations of hypoglycaemia, particularly tachycardia, and non-selective beta-blockers may potentiate insulin-induced hypoglycaemia and delay recovery of serum glucose, which is less likely with a beta1-selective agent; beta-adrenergic blockade may mask clinical signs of hyperthyroidism and abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm. Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, overt cardiac failure, second- or third-degree atrioventricular block and marked sinus bradycardia. In two US placebo-controlled studies, withdrawal for adverse events occurred in 3.3% of patients receiving bisoprolol and 6.8% receiving placebo, and bradycardia, diarrhoea, asthenia, fatigue and sinusitis appeared dose related.
